label: Problem set 5
title: Problem set 5: Wave-particle duality and quantised energy
summary: Practice Lesson 5: the de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p, why heavy objects show no wave behaviour, the Bohr condition 2πr = nλ, and the energy levels and spectra of hydrogen.

intro.text: This set covers the wave nature of matter. De Broglie's idea was simple and startling: every moving particle has a wavelength, λ = h/p. For everyday objects that wavelength is unbelievably tiny; for electrons it is the size of atoms.
We also use the Bohr model of hydrogen, where the electron wave must fit a whole number of wavelengths around its orbit, and the levels follow Eₙ = −13.6 / n² eV.

sections.title: De Broglie waves and the Bohr model
sections.summary: Use λ = h/p and Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV to relate momentum, wavelength and energy levels, and to find photon energies from transitions.
keyPoints: De Broglie wavelength: λ = h / p, and p = mv.
Large mass or speed means large momentum and a very short wavelength.
Bohr condition: the orbit holds a whole number of wavelengths, 2πr = nλ.
Hydrogen levels: Eₙ = −13.6 / n² eV; a transition emits |ΔE|.

blocks.text: To find the de Broglie wavelength, first work out the momentum. For a particle of mass m moving at speed v, p = mv, then λ = h/p. Because h is so small, the wavelength is only noticeable for the lightest particles.

blocks.caption: The de Broglie wavelength and the hydrogen levels

blocks.text: In the Bohr picture the electron is a wave running round the nucleus. It joins up smoothly only when a whole number of wavelengths fits the orbit. That single condition forces the energies into a discrete ladder.

blocks.title: The de Broglie wavelength of a fast electron
blocks.given: An electron (mass 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg) moves at 2.0 × 10⁶ m/s. Find its de Broglie wavelength. Take h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.
blocks.result: The electron wavelength is about 0.36 nm, close to the spacing between atoms, which is why electrons can be diffracted by crystals.

blocks.title: Only electrons and other light particles show it
blocks.body: A cricket ball with p about 3 kg m/s has a wavelength of order 10⁻³⁴ m, far too small to detect. Waves of matter are real for all particles, but only light, fast ones show measurable effects.

questions.question: Why is the wave nature of a thrown cricket ball never noticed?
options: a cricket ball has no wave nature
its momentum is huge, so its de Broglie wavelength is far too small to detect
balls are not made of matter
questions.explanation: λ = h/p. A cricket ball has a large mass and speed, so p is enormous and λ is around 10⁻³⁴ m: utterly undetectable. Electrons, being tiny, have wavelengths the size of atoms.

questions.question: Electrons can produce a diffraction pattern.
questions.explanation: A beam of electrons passed through a thin crystal or a double slit forms a diffraction pattern, exactly as a wave would. This is direct evidence for the de Broglie picture.

questions.question: Find the momentum, in kg m/s, of an electron whose de Broglie wavelength is 0.50 nm = 5.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Take h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.
Find the de Broglie wavelength, in metres, of a proton (mass 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) moving at 1.0 × 10⁵ m/s. Take h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.
questions.explanation: p = mv = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ × 1.0 × 10⁵ = 1.67 × 10⁻²² kg m/s, so λ = h/p = 3.97 × 10⁻¹² m. The heavier proton has a much shorter wavelength than an electron of similar speed.

questions.question: An electron has momentum 2.0 × 10⁻²⁴ kg m/s. Find its kinetic energy, in joules. Take m = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg.
In the Bohr model, the allowed orbits are fixed by:
options: the condition 2πr = nλ, a whole number of wavelengths round the orbit
the mass of the nucleus alone
questions.explanation: The electron wave must join up smoothly as it goes round. That happens only if the circumference holds a whole number of wavelengths, which picks out the allowed orbits.

questions.question: Energy leaves an atom only in fixed amounts, which is why its spectrum is a set of lines.
questions.explanation: Because the energy levels are discrete, differences between them take only certain values. Each allowed difference corresponds to one sharp line in the spectrum.

questions.question: For hydrogen, the ground-state energy is:
questions.explanation: The lowest level of hydrogen, n = 1, lies at −13.6 eV. The negative sign means the electron is bound; the energy needed to remove it completely is 13.6 eV.

questions.question: For hydrogen, Eₙ = −13.6 / n² eV. Find the energy of the n = 3 level, in eV.
Find the energy, in eV, of the photon emitted when hydrogen falls from n = 3 (−1.51 eV) to n = 2 (−3.40 eV). Give the magnitude.
questions.explanation: The photon carries the difference: |−1.51 − (−3.40)| = 1.89 eV. This is the red Hα line of hydrogen.

questions.question: Which statements about de Broglie waves are correct? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Every particle has a de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p; a larger momentum (for example a larger mass) means a shorter wavelength. It is not special to electrons, though only very light particles show measurable effects.

questions.question: The double-slit experiment with single electrons shows that:
questions.explanation: Each electron arrives as a single dot, yet many dots build an interference pattern. That is the wave behaviour of a particle, the heart of wave-particle duality.

questions.question: The de Broglie wavelength of a particle is given by:
questions.explanation: De Broglie's relation links wavelength to momentum through the Planck constant: λ = h/p.

questions.question: Electron diffraction shows that electrons have wave properties.
questions.explanation: The diffraction pattern is a wave phenomenon, so its appearance for electrons shows that they behave as waves.

questions.question: Which are supported by the Bohr model? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The Bohr model gives discrete levels, quantised angular momentum and the hydrogen spectrum. Electron diffraction needs the full wave picture of matter.
